title: A stiff system makes an explicit solver crawl, and a neural ODE has to learn that same right-hand side
summary: Stiffness means one very fast decaying mode forces an explicit method to take tiny steps long after that mode is gone. The step limit comes from the stability region of the method, implicit methods remove it, and an adaptive solver on a stiff problem ends up limited by stability rather than accuracy. A neural ODE learns the right-hand side from data, so its rollouts inherit both the stiffness and the growth of every small error in what it learned.

media.alt: Complex plane of h times lambda. A teal shaded region with a bump on the right is the stable region of the fourth-order Runge-Kutta method, reaching about minus 2.8 on the real axis. A dashed blue circle of radius 1 centred at minus 1 is the Euler region. Orange dots inside are stable step choices at h = 0.5, and a red cross at minus 3 on the real axis lies outside and is unstable.

source.note: Standard numerical analysis. The figure is the design system's synthetic F5.2 render, so no project number is quoted. Every number in the steps and the worked example was computed for this page with SciPy and checked by script; solver counts depend on the tolerances stated.

read_the_figure.question: For which values of the step size times the eigenvalue does a given method decay when the true solution decays, and which method has the larger safe region?
read_the_figure.axes: x: the real part of h times lambda (lambda is an eigenvalue of the equation, h the step). Decaying physical modes have a negative real part and sit on the left. y: the imaginary part, an oscillation of the mode.
look_at: The boundary curve: inside it the numerical solution decays, outside it grows without bound.
How far the region reaches along the negative real axis. Euler reaches -2, RK4 about -2.8; this number is the stiffness limit.
The red cross at -3 on the real axis: outside both regions, so a step that large blows up even though the true solution decays.
Whether the region contains the whole left half-plane. Only then is the method A-stable and free of a step limit for decaying modes.
read_the_figure.proves: A step choice that falls outside the region is certain to give a diverging numerical solution for that linear mode; a choice inside gives decay, not accuracy.
if_wrong: Plotting h lambda for a single eigenvalue and calling the solver stable: every eigenvalue must be inside, so the fastest one decides.
Equal axis scale lost: the Euler circle looks like an ellipse and the reader mistakes where it crosses the axis.
Treating the region as a guarantee for nonlinear problems: it is a local statement about the Jacobian's eigenvalues.
must_check: Stable side shaded and the boundary labelled |R(z)| = 1.
Which method each curve belongs to.
The position of the actual eigenvalues times h, if the plot claims to explain a run.

terms.meaning: A problem with widely separated time scales, where the fast ones have died out but still limit the step of an explicit method.
The largest decay rate of the system divided by the smallest: how many times faster the fastest mode is than the slowest one.
The new value is computed from the old one alone. Cheap per step, but with a step limit set by stability.
The new value appears on both sides, so each step solves an equation. Costlier per step, with no stability limit for decaying modes in the best methods.
The factor by which one step multiplies the solution of the test equation y' = lambda y, a function of z = h lambda.
The set of z for which the numerical solution of the test equation decays: |R(z)| < 1.
Stable for every z with negative real part, so the step never has to be restricted for stability when modes decay.
Backward differentiation formulas: implicit multistep methods of order 1 to 6 that are the standard choice for stiff problems.
A solver that estimates its own local error and changes the step so the error stays near a tolerance.
An ODE whose right-hand side is a neural network with trainable weights, solved with an ordinary integrator and trained so that its solutions match data.
Integrating a learned model from an initial state over many steps, so that errors made early are carried forward.

remember: Test equation: $y'=\lambda y$ with $\operatorname{Re}\lambda<0$. The true solution decays.
Explicit Euler multiplies by $1+h\lambda$ each step; it decays only if $|1+h\lambda|<1$, so for real $\lambda<0$ the step must satisfy $h<2/|\lambda|$.
Implicit Euler multiplies by $1/(1-h\lambda)$ and is stable for every $h$ when $\operatorname{Re}\lambda<0$ (A-stable).
Stiffness ratio is the spread of the decay rates. The fastest mode sets the explicit step limit for the whole run.
BDF methods and implicit Runge-Kutta methods are the stiff solvers. Dahlquist showed that an A-stable multistep method can be at most second order.

A neural ODE learns $f_\theta$; a small error $\varepsilon$ in it grows like $\varepsilon(e^{Lt}-1)/L$ over a rollout, where $L$ is the Lipschitz constant, and saturates at $\varepsilon/|\lambda|$ if the dynamics are contracting.

understand.title: Easy: a fast mode makes you walk in tiny steps
understand.text: Imagine a ball rolling down a gentle hill into a narrow ravine whose walls pull it back very quickly. After one instant the ball is at the ravine's bottom and then drifts slowly along it. A step-by-step method that works from where it is now overshoots the walls unless each step is tiny, even though nothing interesting is happening any more. That is stiffness: the problem is slow, but the method has to behave as if it were fast.

understand.title: Medium: where the step limit comes from
understand.text: Apply Euler to the test equation. The solution is multiplied by the number $1+h\lambda$ each step. If its size is above one, the numerical solution grows, however accurate the step might have looked. For decay at rate 1000 this means $h<0.002$. Any larger step turns a quickly decaying exact solution into a quickly growing numerical one. The method is not inaccurate; it is unstable. Implicit Euler divides by $1-h\lambda$ instead and that factor shrinks when $\lambda$ is negative, for any $h$.

understand.title: Hard: stiff solvers pay per step to take big steps
understand.text: An implicit step solves a nonlinear equation, usually by Newton's method, which needs the Jacobian and a linear solve with $I-hJ$. That is much more work than one explicit step. It pays when the step is thousands of times larger. In the check below a stiff test problem took an explicit RK45 3,567 steps and 21,428 right-hand side evaluations; the implicit Radau method took 35 steps and 292 evaluations plus a Jacobian solve each step. For a non-stiff problem the explicit method is cheaper. Choose by the ratio, not by habit.

understand.title: Hardest: why a neural ODE on stiff data is hard to train
understand.text: The data usually contain a short, violent transient and then a long slow stretch, so most samples carry slow-mode information and the fast mode is learned from very few points. The learned $f_\theta$ must also have a Jacobian with the right widely separated eigenvalues: a small error in the fast eigenvalue's sign or size changes the stability of the rollout. The training loop integrates $f_\theta$ with a solver, and an explicit solver needs steps below $2/|\lambda_{\max}|$ of the current network, which can change during training. The loss landscape is correspondingly badly scaled, with directions that differ in curvature by the stiffness ratio. Standard remedies are an implicit solver, rescaling the variables so the loss sees the slow and fast parts equally, and transforming the state so the eigenvalues are compressed.

steps.title: The test equation
steps.note: Every linear system y' = Ay reduces to copies of this equation along the eigenvectors of A, so one number lambda per mode is enough to judge a method on a linear problem. Atlas S16 example 0 draws the decay.

steps.title: Explicit Euler and its stability region
steps.tex: y_{n+1}=y_n+h\lambda y_n=(1+z)\,y_n,\quad z=h\lambda;\qquad |1+z|<1\ \text{is the disk of radius 1 about }-1
steps.note: The numerical solution decays exactly when the multiplier has size below one. On the real axis that means -2 < h lambda < 0, so for a decay rate |lambda| the step must stay below 2/|lambda|. Checked numerically with lambda = -1000: the multiplier is -0.9 at h = 0.0019 (decays with sign flips), -1.0 at 0.002 (neutral) and -1.1 at 0.0021 (grows).

steps.title: Stiffness ratio and what it costs
steps.note: With rates 1 and 1000 the slow mode would be resolved by steps of order 0.1, but the fast mode caps the step at 0.002: a run to T = 10 needs at least 5000 steps, 50 times more than accuracy alone asks for. The ratio 1000 is the stiffness ratio. Atlas S32 example 0 shows an explicit Euler run on a stiff decay.

steps.title: Implicit Euler is stable for every step
steps.note: For any z with negative real part the expression x squared minus 2x plus y squared is positive (each term is non-negative and -2x is positive), so |1 - z| exceeds 1 and the multiplier is below 1. The stability region is the whole left half-plane and more: the method is A-stable. Verified symbolically; at lambda = -1000 and h = 0.0025 the multiplier is 0.286 rather than Euler's -1.5.

steps.title: The implicit step is an equation to solve
steps.note: Newton's method applied to the step equation, with J the Jacobian of f. One linear solve with I - hJ per Newton iteration is the extra price of an implicit step. For a linear problem a single iteration is exact.

steps.title: BDF2 and its order
steps.note: Backward differentiation uses the past values to fit a parabola and imposes the ODE at the new point. Checked on y' = -y to T = 1: halving h from 0.1 to 0.05 to 0.025 reduced the error by factors 3.80 and 3.92, so it is second order. For roots of its characteristic polynomial (1.5 - z) w^2 - 2w + 0.5 = 0 the largest size over 100,000 random points with negative real part was below 1 in the check, consistent with A-stability (Dahlquist 1963 proved A-stable multistep methods have order at most 2).

steps.title: Adaptive step size and the stability ceiling
steps.note: The local error of a method of order p scales as h to the p + 1, so the controller aims the next step at the tolerance (Euler: halving h cut the local error by 3.93, near 4). On y' = -1000 (y - cos t) - sin t the explicit RK45 settled at median steps of 0.0028, close to its real-axis stability limit of about 3.3 over 1000, even though the solution cos t is smooth: the step is limited by stability, not accuracy. That is what the step-size-against-ceiling plot diagnoses.

steps.title: A neural ODE learns the right-hand side
steps.note: The unknown is the function f, parametrised by weights theta; the solver is part of the model, so its stability and step control matter as much as in any simulation. The Jacobian of f_theta at a point has eigenvalues, and those eigenvalues are the model's own stiffness ratio there.

steps.title: Error growth in a rollout
steps.note: Gronwall's inequality: if the learned f is within epsilon of the true one and the field's Lipschitz constant is L, a rollout error cannot exceed this. For epsilon = 0.01, L = 2 and t = 5 the bound is 110, while for a contracting mode with lambda = -1000 the error saturates at epsilon over |lambda| = 1e-5. The exact solution of the linear case was confirmed symbolically. The bound is a worst case; actual errors are often much smaller.

worked.title: What happens to Euler on a decay at rate 1000 with a step of 0.0025?
worked.problem: Solve $y'=-1000y$, $y(0)=1$, with explicit Euler and with implicit Euler at $h=0.0025$. Find the multiplier of each, the value after 20 steps ($t=0.05$) and the largest stable Euler step. How many steps would Euler need to reach $T=10$ at that step?

solution.text: Implicit Euler multiplier at the same step.
Largest stable Euler step and the step count to $T=10$.

worked.answer: Euler: multiplier -1.5, so the solution flips sign and grows to about 3,300 after only 20 steps although the true solution has decayed to 1e-22. Implicit Euler: multiplier 0.286, decays at any step. Euler needs h below 0.002, so at least 5000 steps to reach T = 10. On the smooth stiff test problem y' = -1000(y - cos t) - sin t over [0, 10] with rtol 1e-6, SciPy's RK45 used 3,567 steps and 21,428 evaluations, Radau 35 steps and 292, BDF 168 steps and 438 evaluations.

analyze.q: On the stability-region plot the red cross at -3 lies outside both the Euler circle and the RK4 region. What are two ways to make that mode stable, and what does each cost?
analyze.hint: Reduce h, or change the method. How many more steps, or how much more work per step?

analyze.q: A run of an adaptive explicit solver on a smooth stiff problem shows the step size flat at a constant value long after the transient. What does the flat line say and how would you confirm it?
analyze.hint: Compare the flat step with 3 over the largest |eigenvalue| of the Jacobian.

analyze.q: A neural-ODE rollout matches the training transient but diverges slowly later while the data stay smooth. Name two possible causes related to this page.
analyze.hint: Think about the learned Jacobian's slow eigenvalue, and about the solver's step used at test time.

evaluate.q: A report says 'our model is stable because the solver did not blow up.' What would you want to see before accepting that for a stiff problem?
evaluate.hint: Solver, tolerances, step history, eigenvalues of the learned Jacobian along the trajectory.

evaluate.q: Is a bigger stability region always better? Compare a method that is A-stable with one that has a larger but bounded region and higher order.
evaluate.hint: Dahlquist: A-stable multistep methods have order at most 2. What about accuracy per step and cost per step?

create: Design a test that shows whether a learned right-hand side is stiff in the same way as the true one: which quantity do you compute along the trajectory and what plot shows it?
You must train on data with a fast transient followed by a slow tail. Sketch a sampling scheme in time, and a loss scaling, so the transient is not drowned out.
Write down a short checklist for choosing between RK45 and a BDF method for a new problem using a cheap test run.

checks.q: What exactly makes explicit Euler unstable on y' = -1000 y with h = 0.01?
checks.answer: $z=h\lambda=-10$, the multiplier is $1+z=-9$, so each step multiplies the size by 9 while the exact solution decays. The method is not inaccurate; it is outside its stability region, which on the real axis ends at $z=-2$.

checks.q: A system has rates 0.5 and 400. What is the stiffness ratio and the largest stable Euler step, and how many steps does Euler need for T = 20?
Why does implicit Euler give a correct decay but a poor transient at a large step?
checks.hint: Stable does not mean accurate. Compare 1/(1 - z) with e^z at z = -10.
checks.answer: At $z=-10$ the exact one-step factor is $e^{-10}=4.5\times10^{-5}$ and implicit Euler gives $1/11=0.091$. It decays but far too slowly in that step: the fast transient is damped inaccurately. It is first order, so accuracy needs a step set by the solution, with stability left to the method.

checks.q: A teammate switches to a stiff solver and the run takes 10 times longer. Is that a sign that the problem is not stiff?
checks.hint: What does each implicit step cost, and how many fewer steps were taken?
checks.answer: Quite possibly. An implicit method pays a Jacobian and a linear solve per step, so on a non-stiff problem where an explicit method already takes steps set by accuracy it is slower. The test is the step history: if the explicit solver's steps are flat at a stability ceiling the problem is stiff; if they track the accuracy and vary with the solution it is not.

checks.q: You have a learned right-hand side f_theta and want to know if it is safe to integrate with an explicit method at step 0.01. What do you compute?
checks.hint: The eigenvalues of the Jacobian of f_theta along representative states, times h.
checks.answer: Evaluate the Jacobian of $f_\theta$ with automatic differentiation at states sampled along the trajectories of interest, compute its eigenvalues, and check that $h\lambda$ lies inside the stability region of the method for every one (for Euler, $|1+h\lambda|<1$). Plot the largest $|\lambda|$ against time on a log scale: if $0.01\,|\lambda_{\max}|$ exceeds the region's real-axis reach, use a smaller step or an implicit method.
